script:
Good morning, and welcome to your market briefing for Friday 25 September.

We begin in New York, where Wall Street closed higher as technology led a late rally. The S&P 500 finished up zero point six percent. The Nasdaq Composite did better again, up one point one percent. The Dow Jones added zero point two percent. Chipmakers led the gains, with Nvidia up three point four percent on heavy volume. Apple also finished firmer, up one point two percent. JPMorgan Chase added zero point four percent. Not everything joined in. Tesla ended the session down two point one percent. In bond markets, the US ten-year Treasury yield eased to four point one two percent. Energy was the laggard on the day, with West Texas Intermediate crude slipping one point three percent. So the picture from the United States is one of a market carried by the big technology names, with softer oil prices weighing on the energy side of the ledger, and a slightly easier tone in government bond yields as the session drew to a close.

Over in London, the mood was more subdued. The FTSE 100 edged lower, down zero point three percent, as miners and oil weighed on the index. The more domestically focused FTSE 250 went the other way, up a slim zero point one percent. Among the individual names, BP fell one point eight percent, alongside those weaker crude prices. HSBC was also softer, down zero point six percent. On the positive side of the board, AstraZeneca rose one point five percent, which helped cushion the index from a deeper fall. Vodafone added zero point nine percent. In currencies, the pound held steady against the US dollar at one point three four. So London ended with a split personality. The large-cap index was held back by its resources and energy exposure, while healthcare provided some offset, and the mid-cap index managed to inch ahead.

That brings us home to our own region, where the ASX is set to open with a cautious lead from offshore. Local futures point to a flat to slightly positive start when the ASX 200 opens at ten o'clock AEST. At eleven thirty AEST we get Australian job vacancies data. That is the quarterly release from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and it will be watched for signs of a cooling labour market. Miners are in focus all day, with overnight moves in iron ore and copper setting the tone for BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue. And across the Tasman, New Zealand's monthly trade balance from Stats New Zealand lands at eight forty-five NZST, ahead of the NZX open.

That is your snapshot ahead of the opening bell. This briefing is AI-generated general information only. It is not financial advice.
